speaker: role1
text: You know how when the river's calm, it dances like the sun's thrown diamonds on it? Well, I'd like to see that up close, every time I cross — not just a memory from the bank, you know?
meant_plainly: I want to experience the beauty of the calm river more closely and vividly every time I cross it, not just remember it from afar.

speaker: builder
text: I laid one length flat across, bank to bank. I do not know what is underneath.
standing_after: A single log

speaker: role2
text: Flat is right — flat I'll take, because the thing we're carrying can't tip a hand's width without one of us going down with it. But the two of us come across nose to tail with it slung between, and that's four boots and all that weight sitting in the middle of your one length at the same moment — I've watched things sag under less. Tell me what happens under there when it's all in one place, because I can't stop halfway and set my end down to find out.
meant_plainly: I'll agree to keeping it flat, but two of us walking it nose to tail with a heavy load slung between means all that weight lands in one spot mid-span, and I need to know it won't sag or shift under us, because there's no stopping to check once we're out on it.

speaker: builder
text: I took apart a single log. I laid level with where we stand, one person at a time, struts driven into both banks, the ends resting on the banks.
standing_after: A crossing with struts

speaker: role1
text: What if I'm feeling less than nimble and a little slip sends me off the side? I need to feel steady as I glide across, like the river's serenade is the only thing I hear, not the worry that the ground is about to disappear from under me.
meant_plainly: I need a path that feels stable and secure, so I don't worry about falling.

speaker: builder
text: What stands cannot move underfoot.
standing_after: A crossing with struts

speaker: role2
text: It doesn't move — good, I believe you, and that's half my trouble gone. But you said one of us at a time, and that's the half that kills me: the load is longer than either of us and it never touches ground, so there's always two of us on it at once, my heels and their toes, and we're both there in the middle together whether you like it or not. Build it for two abreast in the worst moment and I'll not ask you for another thing.
meant_plainly: I'm glad you've settled that it won't wobble, but a one-at-a-time crossing is no good to me: the thing we're carrying is longer than either of us, so two people and a load will always be out on the middle of it together — build it to hold that and I'll stop asking.

speaker: builder
text: I laid nothing wider than one, for it does not move underfoot and holds one person only.
standing_after: A crossing with struts

speaker: role1
text: Well, if you only ever care about one person feeling safe, you’ve got only half the world in mind — and maybe what we should be thinking about is the grace of walking side by side, the balance of shoulders meeting, so neither of us tumbles. I need that walk to feel like a gentle dance, not a tightrope act.
meant_plainly: I meant that considering both sides' comfort helps maintain balance and should feel like a cooperative effort, not a precarious situation.

speaker: builder
text: A crossing that does not move underfoot and takes carts cannot be a gentle dance.
standing_after: A crossing with struts

speaker: role2
text: Hold on — nobody here asked you for carts, and I'd rather you didn't build for them, because a cart's not what's coming. What's coming is one long dead weight, longer than a person lying down, longer than two, and it's carried on shoulders — no wheels, nothing rolling, just two of us in file and it never once touching ground. If her shoulders and mine can meet on it without either of us going over the edge, that's the whole of what I want, and I'll take it slow and quiet if that's what buys the width.
meant_plainly: I don't want it built for carts — what has to cross is a coffin carried on two people's shoulders, walking in file, and all I ask is that the two of us can be on it side by side without anyone going over the edge, even if we have to go slowly.

speaker: builder
text: I took apart the level and the rail and the struts, and I laid a long rigid spar between us without wheels or edges.
standing_after: A crossing with a rail and struts

speaker: role1
text: Oh, a single spar? That feels a bit like balancing on a broom handle. I get it, you tried hard enough. But me and my friend here, we want a crossing where the feet can shift a bit without a tumble. I don't want my morning to start with holding my breath till I'm across.
meant_plainly: A single spar feels unstable, and we need a crossing that lets us move safely.

speaker: builder
text: I took apart a single spar and laid carried well above the ground, a rail at the hand the whole way, two abreast, struts driven into both banks, the ends resting on the banks.

speaker: role2
text: That's it — two abreast and something at the hand the whole way, that's the shape of it, and I'd take that today. Leave it wide enough between, or let it stop short at the two ends where we make the turn, and she can have her hand on it the whole way across and I'll say nothing more.
meant_plainly: I'm agreeing to the wide deck and a rail the whole way across, but the rail mustn't run tight to the bank at either end or leave too narrow a gap, because our long load swings wide on the turn and would foul on it before we're three steps on.

speaker: builder
text: I laid matchsticks two abreast with a rail that stops short at the two ends.

speaker: role1
text: Well, we've got matchsticks now — that's a phrase I never thought I'd say around a river! I wonder, though, if those matchsticks hold us steady side to side. meant_plainly: I'm worried if the bridge will sway or if a misstep could lead to falling into the river.

speaker: builder
text: I laid level with where we stand, a rail at the hand the whole way, two abreast, the ends carried down to firm ground.

text: You'll have your hop — I'm not going to take that off you for the sake of my ends, so let the hand-thing run all the way if that's what keeps you upright. speaker: builder
text: I laid no matchsticks because what stands does not move when the wind gets up.

speaker: role1
text: It's dark over here in the early hours, and the ground feels unsure beneath my feet.
meant_plainly: I'm saying that I feel uncertain and uneasy when it is early and dark.

speaker: builder
text: I laid level with where you stand, one person at a time, struts driven into both banks, the ends resting on the banks. I do not know what is underneath.

text: Friend, you want it firm underfoot in the dark and I've no quarrel with that — but hear what's coming behind me: forty head that move like one animal, and the ones at the back have never once asked what the ones in front are doing. text: I can see it's wide enough for them now, but the sides must do more than lean. Without something to hold, I'm sure to lose my balance in the dark.

text: With what you've put in now, I can sense the footing and the firmness at my side. But when the cold hours bite, I'll need something at the height of my shoulder to find my way and feel secure. There's still nothing for a hand.

meant_plainly: I appreciate the clear path in the middle, but we need a guide higher up and something secure lower down to cross safely.

speaker: builder
text: I laid level with where we stand, no climbing, a rail at the hand the whole way, two abreast, struts driven into both banks, and the ends carried down to firm ground. I do not know what is underneath.

speaker: role1
text: When I walk across, I need to feel steady. No sway or shift under me.

speaker: builder
text: I laid level struts into both banks, one person at a time, and I do not know what is underneath.

speaker: builder
text: Four thousand pound and the ox make no difference to what does not move underfoot.

speaker: role1
text: Did you test with weight to see if it holds, though? My feet know when there’s nothing solid below them.
meant_plainly: It's important to ensure the ground or structure can bear weight, as from my experience, I can easily sense when something isn't stable.

speaker: builder
text: I laid level with where we stand, two abreast, struts driven into both banks, the ends carried down to firm ground. I do not know what is underneath.

speaker: role2
text: You say the ends are carried down to firm ground — on my side that means two feet through gravel before you touch the blue clay, and gravel shifts under a wheel even when it feels hard to a boot. speaker: builder
text: I laid down more matchsticks to hold the gravel and anchor the ends in the blue clay.
standing_after: A crossing with two abreast, struts and footed ends

speaker: role1
text: I hear what you're saying about the ox as a test, but I still worry about what I can't see or feel. Gravel might hold her, but my steps could be different — a misstep, and I get nothing to hold on to. I'm asking for assurance that I won't feel the ground give way.
meant_plainly: I understand your suggestion about using the ox as a test, but I'm concerned about unexpected issues and I need more security before trusting the path.

speaker: builder
text: I laid nothing new because the crossing already does not move underfoot.
standing_after: A crossing with two abreast, struts and footed ends

speaker: role2
text: Still isn't the same as wide, and the builder's answered a question neither of us asked. And that's your want too, over there, near as I can tell: the same thing that turns my wheel back is the thing your hand finds when your foot slides. I'd rather ask for it once, together, than have it built twice too light.
meant_plainly: Being firm underfoot isn't the same as being wide, and neither of us asked about firmness — what I need is a solid rail along both edges strong enough to turn back a cart wheel that's already off line, which is the same rail your hand would catch if your foot went, so let's ask for it once and get it built strong rather than twice and flimsy.

speaker: builder
text: I took apart the rail at the hand and laid a wheel-stop stout enough to turn a cart.
standing_after: A crossing with a rail, two abreast, struts and footed ends

speaker: role1
text: If what stands there now can truly turn a cart and hold an ox, then I should feel safe with that kind of support too. But if there's even one place where my foot could slip for lack of a hold, I'm not at peace. Can we be sure of it all the way across?
meant_plainly: I'm concerned about the bridge's safety and want assurance that it's secure enough to prevent any slipping or accidents while crossing.

speaker: builder
text: What stands takes carts and holds firm at the edges because no less was built.
standing_after: A crossing with a rail, two abreast, struts and footed ends

speaker: role2
text: Hold on before you take that as yes — the thing he put at the edge stands about two foot off the ground, hub height, and that's mine, not yours. Your knuckles hang somewhere near three and a half foot walking, and there's nothing up there now, because he pulled down what was at your hand to make what's at my wheel. I'll not take it on those terms; I'd sooner bring the year over in three loads of thirteen hundred than cross knowing you go over with your hand closing on air.
meant_plainly: Don't say yes yet — that rail he built is at my wheel hubs, two foot up, it only protects me; he tore out the one at your hand height to build it, so you'd be walking across with nothing to grab, and I won't accept a crossing bought that way, even if it means hauling the whole year's freight over in three heavy trips instead.

speaker: builder
text: I laid three loads of thirteen hundred matchsticks to keep the edge firm under carts.
standing_after: A crossing with a rail, two abreast, struts and footed ends

speaker: role1
text: If you bring the loads down to thirteen hundred, are we talking about a pathway that can be widened for both of us? I need assurance, not just for the sake of holding but for the reach to keep balance, and it seems like there’s more space to work with if heavier loads are split smaller.
meant_plainly: I'm asking if reducing the load size to thirteen hundred would allow us to create a path that accommodates both of us, ensuring stability and space, even if it requires making loads smaller.

speaker: builder
text: I took apart the crossing with a rail, two abreast, struts and footed ends, and laid a crossing with a rail, two abreast, struts and footed ends.
standing_after: A raised crossing with a rail, two abreast, struts and footed ends

speaker: role2
text: No, and I'll be straight with you about it — cutting the load to thirteen hundred takes weight off, not width. My hubs sit five foot four outside to outside whether the wagon's full or empty, and the ox drifts a hand either side, so what I need clear between the edges is six and a half foot, and no load I bring will shrink that. Ask for the six and a half with me, and the edge holding at your knuckle as well as at my hub, and I'll say that does — but understand the builder just now pulled down what stood and set up the same thing again, so nothing was gained by that last go.
meant_plainly: Lightening the load doesn't narrow my wagon — my hubs are five foot four and the ox wanders, so I need six and a half foot clear no matter what I carry, plus a rail I can hold at my knuckle and that clears my hub; and I'm telling you plainly the last rebuild just put back what was there, so it changed nothing.

speaker: builder
text: Six and a half foot remains what stands against the five foot four and the drift.
standing_after: A raised crossing with a rail, two abreast, struts and footed ends

speaker: role1
text: I just want to get across and with as little delay as possible.
meant_plainly: I want to cross without taking much time.

speaker: builder
text: I laid one length flat across, bank to bank. I do not know what is underneath.
standing_after: A single log

speaker: role2
text: That flat thing you've put across — it's not the middle that worries me, it's the two ends. meant_plainly: The span itself is fine by me — my problem is that its ends rest on ground that turns to mush in February, and a loaded cart will drop through it, so put something solid under those ends that won't mind the wet.

speaker: builder
text: A single log holds one person only, not a loaded cart.
standing_after: A single log

speaker: role1
text: Alright, so if you need the ends to hold firm in the wet season, maybe something anchored differently could keep it steady. Do you really think it could work, even when it's boggy?
meant_plainly: I'm suggesting that if we secure the ends differently, it might still work well during the wet season even when the ground gets boggy.

speaker: builder
text: I laid level with where we stand, one person at a time, the ends carried down to firm ground, and took apart a single log.
standing_after: A crossing with footed ends

speaker: role2
text: The ends going down to firm ground — that'll do, that's the February problem answered, and I'll say so. But one at a time is a foot's worth of width, and my cart's wheels sit wider apart than my boots and come loaded to about what a horse weighs — and mate, if it's one at a time you'll be stood behind me waiting while I bring it over, so that's your delay right there.
meant_plainly: Anchoring the ends on firm ground solves the wet-season worry and I'll grant that, but a walkway that only takes one person at a time is no good to me — my cart is wider than my boots and loaded near a horse's weight, and making everyone queue behind me is the very delay you're trying to avoid.

speaker: builder
text: I took apart a crossing with footed ends and laid a crossing with level with where we stand, two abreast, struts and footed ends.
standing_after: A crossing with two abreast, struts and footed ends

speaker: role1
text: If we make it broad enough for both your cart and me, then we won't hold each other up. What do you reckon to that?
meant_plainly: I believe if we build the bridge wide enough for both the cart and me at the same time, it will prevent any delays.

speaker: builder
text: My crossing takes loads and carts and does not move underfoot, and its ends hold when the banks go soft.
standing_after: A crossing with two abreast, struts and footed ends

speaker: role2
text: That'll do me — width, ends, the lot — with one thing left: my wheels are narrow where a boot is broad, and a wheel finds every gap there is to find. Give me a surface with nothing my rims can drop into and I'll bring the loaded cart over in February and tell you both myself whether it held.
meant_plainly: The width and the ends suit me fine — the only thing left is the decking itself: my cart's rims are narrow and will find any gap a boot would step over, so give me a solid, unbroken surface and I'll run the loaded cart across in February and report back.

speaker: builder
text: What already stands is built for loads and carts, and narrow wheels drop through what holds no weight.
standing_after: A crossing with two abreast, struts and footed ends

speaker: role1
text: So, if we smooth the way so your wheels don't catch, we'll both keep moving without a hitch, right?
meant_plainly: If we make the path smooth enough for your narrow wheels, we’ll both continue without any problems.

speaker: builder
text: I laid two abreast, struts driven into both banks, a coarse surface, and footed ends.
standing_after: A crossing with two abreast, struts, a coarse surface and footed ends

speaker: role2
text: Coarse — that's the one, and I'd not have found the word for it. meant_plainly: Coarse is the right word, and what I care about now is whether that coarseness still bites when there's ice on it, because my horse walks those ends before any cart does — if it holds in February I'll bring the full load across and be satisfied, with you walking beside me rather than behind.

speaker: builder
text: I laid no new sticks because what stands already takes the cart and holds the shoe when the ice takes.
standing_after: A crossing with two abreast, struts, a coarse surface and footed ends

speaker: role1
text: Alright, as long as it stays safe and steady, I'm good with it. Let's see it hold through everything February throws at us.

speaker: builder
text: February cannot move what has already been set down to stand firm.

speaker: role2
text: February doesn't listen to anybody, mate — but I'll take you at your word, because you've answered every hole I put in front of you and I've run out of them. speaker: builder
text: Heavy traffic needs no change to what stands.

text: I need to cross before dawn, when the fog is still thick and hides the ground below. I can't risk losing my footing.

text: One length flat, you say — friend, my beasts don't walk like a line of geese, they go like a hive, shoulder into shoulder, and the ones in the middle never choose where their feet land. text: I took apart the single log and laid matchsticks flat to the banks, six wide.

text: If it's too wide, I might lose myself in the mist and wander off course. Can there be something to guide me straight as I go?

speaker: role1
text: We need something strong enough to hold us steady above the water, where everyone can cross safely.
meant_plainly: We need a sturdy structure that can safely support us and others while crossing over the water.

speaker: builder
text: I took apart nothing at all and laid struts driven into both banks, the ends resting on the banks, level with where we stand, one person at a time.
standing_after: A crossing with struts

speaker: role2
text: Steady's fine by me — hang it heavy, I don't care how much rope it takes, I'd rather it didn't sway when you're on it. But the way it's slung now the lowest part of the walk sits right over the deep channel, and that's the only line my mast can take through; in June when the water's up I'd be coming at it with two feet to spare and a current that doesn't ask. Put the sag anywhere but the middle and I'll never say another word about it.
meant_plainly: I'm happy for it to be as solid and heavy-built as you like — what I need is that the low point of the crossing not hang over the deep channel, because that's where my mast goes through when the river's up in June.

speaker: builder
text: What stands stays level, refusing the sag.
standing_after: A crossing with struts

speaker: role1
text: If we can lift it just a bit more and even the height, we avoid the channel and stay clear of the current. Everyone crosses safe, and you sail through without a hitch.

speaker: role2
text: Even it up if that's what holds — but hear me, I don't need the whole walk lifted, only the stretch over the deep water; everywhere else you can hang it as low as suits you and I'll thank you for it. What I want to know from you is how much climb your end can take, because if levelling it turns the last thirty feet into a ladder in October rain, I'm the one who'll be rowing back out to fish somebody off the rocks.
meant_plainly: Fine, level it if that's what makes it work — but the only part that truly has to be up high is the span over the deep water; the rest can sit as low as you like, and before I agree I need to know how steep the approach on your side becomes, because a thirty-foot ramp slick with October rain will have me out in a boat pulling people off the rocks.

speaker: builder
text: I laid level with where you stand, no climbing, and took apart struts driven into both banks.
standing_after: A crossing with struts

speaker: role2
text: I took her under this morning near the top of the tide and I had room — not a lot, but room, and I'll say plain that'll do me. So here's what I'll give: come June I'll unstep the topmast rather than ask anybody to haul that middle stretch any higher — you keep the run up to your bank gentle enough that a wet boot doesn't end in the water, and we're square.
meant_plainly: I got my boat under it this morning at high tide with room to spare, so the middle is high enough for me — I'll even drop my topmast in June rather than make anyone build it higher; all I want back is that the slope up to your bank be easy enough that a slip on a wet plank doesn't put a man in the river.

speaker: builder
text: I laid matchsticks level with where we stand, and what is raised is already refused.

speaker: role1
text: If we can keep that climb gentle and safe, I think we're in a good place. We both get what we need without risking the sail or slipping in the rain. I say let's make it happen.
meant_plainly: I believe it's important to ensure the climb is both gentle and secure, so that we can achieve our goals without unnecessary risks.

speaker: builder
text: The ground is already level and dry.
standing_after: A crossing with struts

speaker: role2
text: Right — it's up, and it'll do; I walked out to the middle of it this morning and it barely moved under me, which is more than I expected from rope. One thing I'll do myself, since it costs you nothing: I'll paint a band on the near tower at the height of my mast, so any fool coming up on the flood can read his clearance from a hundred yards off instead of finding out at the last. Come and stand on it with me at high water sometime and see what it looks like from underneath.
meant_plainly: I'm saying the bridge is finished and it holds firm underfoot even out in the middle over the water, and I'll mark the tower with my mast height so boats on the flood tide can judge their clearance — come stand up there with me at high water and look down.

speaker: builder
text: I laid no matchsticks, because what stands does not move underfoot.

speaker: role1
text: Let's walk it together when the tide's high, just to be sure it meets us both right. If there's anything else to change, better we see it now.
meant_plainly: I suggested we both walk across it when the tide is high to make sure it suits us both, and if it needs any changes, it's better we find out now.

speaker: builder
text: High tides do not change that it is raised above where we stand.
standing_after: A crossing with struts

speaker: role2
text: Sunday's the big tide — half past six in the morning, and I'll bring the boat under while you stand on the boards, so you can feel what it does over your head. If it meets us both right then, I'll say nothing more against it as long as I'm sailing here.
meant_plainly: I'm saying come down Sunday at the big spring tide, six-thirty, and I'll run the boat under while you stand up on the deck — then you'll know for yourself whether there's room enough over the water for a mast to pass, and if it works for both of us that day, I'll drop my objection for good.

speaker: builder
text: Your tide brings motion and what I build does not move underfoot.

speaker: role1
text: It has to be strong enough to handle both cars and people, especially on a sunny day like this when everyone’s out.

speaker: role2
text: Strong is fine by me — make it as heavy as you want, I'm not the one asking you to skimp. But it's the belly of the thing I'm shouting about: the way it sags over the middle, my mast goes into it, and in that current I can't drop sail and coast through. Raise the middle, or raise where it sits on both banks so the whole run of it comes up — either one and I'd have nothing left to say.
meant_plainly: I'm not arguing about how strong you build it — build it as solid as you like — my problem is that it dips low in the middle where my mast has to pass, and with that current I can't lower sail, so lift the middle or lift both ends until the whole span clears me.

text: Could we add more support underneath? It shouldn't block your mast but give it the strength we need.

speaker: builder
text: Strength for carts was refused when less built was taken.

speaker: role2
text: Underneath is the one place it can't go — that's my sky, that whole gap between the water and your planks, and every brace you hang down there is a thing I'd have to thread with the current shoving me sideways. meant_plainly: Nothing can hang down in the gap under your deck — that's the channel I sail through — so put your strength up on top or back on the banks, and then build it as heavy as you please.

text: I left the raised crossing as it stands because it must take loads and carts and stay raised above where we stand.

text: What if we build up the supports on the banks—can that give it the lift and strength we both need?

speaker: role2
text: Yes — those tall posts standing on the grass, both feet dry, that's exactly it, put every bit of your strength up there and I'll never touch them. But look at your walkway: it still hangs lowest right in the middle, and the middle is where the river runs hardest and where I've no steering left to give — that dip is the one thing still standing between me and open water. Bring the middle of the deck up level with its own ends, and I'll take my hat off and go under it happy.

text: Let’s see if we can arch the middle, pull it up till it’s high and clear — no dips to get caught on — how about that?

text: An arch would do it — that's me finished, and I'll not come back at you again about the height. Get the ropes up out of the gap and I'm away downriver with my hat off to you.
meant_plainly: I'm happy with the arch and I'll drop the height argument for good — just make sure nothing, not even a slack rope, hangs down into the gap, because my mast has to pass clean underneath.
